question: How did H5N1 bird flu affect US dairy cattle and poultry in 2025?
text:
In 2025, H5N1 bird flu **sickened dairy cows and disrupted milk production on affected farms**, but it hit poultry much harder: **more than 50 million birds were in affected flocks**, and losses among laying hens helped drive egg prices to a record high. ([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/status-report-livestock-edition-508.pdf?utm_source=openai))

- **Dairy cattle:** USDA recorded **171 herd detections in 2025, down from 917 in 2024**, the first year H5N1 was detected in U.S. dairy cattle. Sick cows could lose their appetite and produce sharply less milk, but herds generally weren’t culled as poultry flocks were. USDA used bulk-milk testing to track infections and identified separate wildlife spillovers into herds in Nevada, Arizona, and Wisconsin. Despite losses on affected farms, **total U.S. milk production rose 2.6%** from 2024, and FDA testing supported the safety of pasteurized milk. ([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/avian/avian-influenza/hpai-detections/hpai-confirmed-cases-livestock?utm_source=openai))
- **Poultry:** The virus struck commercial and backyard flocks, with about **45 million birds affected by the end of June alone**. Infected flocks were generally culled to stop the spread, so the number of birds affected is not a count of birds that died from the virus itself. Egg-laying hens were especially hard hit: U.S. table-egg production fell **about 4%** from 2024, and the average retail price reached a record **$6.23 per dozen in March 2025** before easing. ([aphis.usda.gov](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/hpai-epi-report-fy25-q3.pdf?utm_source=openai))
